q: Counting its overseas territories, which country spans the most time zones?
why: France, with 12 (13 counting its Antarctic claim). Territories from French Polynesia to Réunion scatter it around the globe. Russia has 11 across its mainland; China uses just one for the whole country.

statement: Africa is wider from east to west than it is long from north to south.
why: False. It is roughly 8,000 km north to south and about 7,400 km east to west. Common maps distort Africa to look smaller than it is — it could fit the US, China, India and most of Europe inside it.

title: Alaska is the westernmost, northernmost and easternmost US state.
detail: Its Aleutian Islands stretch across the 180° meridian, so the farthest of them sit in the Eastern Hemisphere — technically making Alaska the most easterly state too.

q: What is the capital of Turkey?
why: Ankara. Atatürk moved the capital there in 1923, away from Istanbul, the old imperial capital — which remains Turkey's largest city and straddles Europe and Asia.

q: How deep is the deepest known point in the ocean, the Challenger Deep?
why: About 11 km (roughly 10,900 m), in the Mariana Trench. Drop Everest into it and its peak would still be over 2 km underwater. The pressure is about 1,000 times that at the surface.

statement: The summit of Mount Everest is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's center.
why: False — that's Chimborazo in Ecuador. Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo's peak, near the equator, sits about 2 km farther from the center even though Everest is higher above sea level.

q: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
why: Vatican City, at about 0.44 km² — smaller than many city parks. Monaco, the second smallest, is about 2 km².

title: Canada has the longest coastline of any country — over 200,000 km.
detail: Its tens of thousands of Arctic islands account for much of it. Walking it at 20 km a day would take more than 30 years.

q: Which country contains more lakes than the rest of the world combined, by some counts?
why: Canada. Glaciers scoured its landscape during the last ice age, leaving millions of lakes. By common estimates, it holds over half of the world's lakes.

statement: The Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye.
why: False. It is only a few meters wide. From the Moon, about 384,000 km away, even whole continents are hard to make out in detail. Astronauts have said it is barely visible even from low Earth orbit.

q: Which of these African countries was never colonized by a European power, apart from a brief Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941?
why: Ethiopia. It defeated an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, and its independence made it a symbol of African sovereignty. Liberia is the other country usually cited.

q: Which is the driest non-polar desert on Earth?
why: The Atacama in Chile. Some weather stations there have never recorded rain. NASA tests Mars rovers there because its soil is so lifeless.

title: Australia is wider than the Moon.
detail: Australia stretches about 4,000 km from east to west. The Moon's diameter is about 3,475 km.

q: Which country has the largest population in Africa?
why: Nigeria, with over 200 million people. By mid-century it is projected to be among the most populous countries on Earth.

statement: The Pacific Ocean is larger than all of Earth's land area combined.
why: True. At about 165 million km², it exceeds the total land area of about 149 million km² and covers roughly a third of the planet's surface.

q: Why is the sky blue?
options: Air scatters short blue wavelengths of sunlight much more than red ones
The Sun emits mostly blue light
why: Rayleigh scattering. Scattering grows sharply as wavelength shrinks, so blue light bounces around the sky. At sunset, light crosses more air and the blue is scattered away, leaving reds.

statement: Sound travels faster in water than in air.
why: True — about four times faster. Roughly 1,480 m/s in water versus 343 m/s in air. Molecules packed closely together pass vibrations along more quickly.

q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
why: Nitrogen, about 78%. Oxygen is about 21% and argon about 0.9%. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%, yet it has an outsized effect on climate.

title: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh around a billion tonnes on Earth.
detail: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 km across. Atoms are crushed so completely that protons and electrons merge into neutrons.

q: Which organ uses about 20% of your body's energy at rest, despite being about 2% of your body weight?
why: The brain. Keeping billions of neurons ready to fire is expensive — about 20 watts, roughly a dim light bulb, running continuously.
False. Beyond sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, we sense balance, body position (proprioception), temperature, pain and internal states like hunger. Counts range from about nine to over twenty.

q: On which planet is a single day longer than its year?
why: Venus. It rotates once every 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in 225. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.

title: Botanically, bananas are berries — and strawberries are not.
detail: A berry develops from a single flower's ovary with seeds inside, which bananas, grapes and even tomatoes fit. Strawberries carry their seeds on the outside, so they don't qualify.

q: If you uncoiled all the DNA in a single human cell, how long would it be?
why: About 2 meters, packed into a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimeter wide. The DNA in all your cells together would stretch to the Sun and back many times.

statement: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
why: False. Tall, isolated structures are struck repeatedly. The Empire State Building is hit about 20 to 25 times a year.

q: At the summit of Everest, roughly what temperature does water boil at?
why: About 70°C. Lower air pressure lets water molecules escape more easily. That is why cooking pasta at altitude takes longer — the water never gets as hot.

title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
detail: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one through the body. Their blood uses copper-based hemocyanin to carry oxygen, which turns blue when oxygenated.

q: What causes Earth's seasons?
options: Earth being closer to the Sun in summer
The tilt of Earth's axis, about 23.4°
why: Axial tilt. Each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight and longer days while tilted toward the Sun. Distance barely matters — which is why the hemispheres have opposite seasons.

statement: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
why: True. Perihelion falls around January 3, in the middle of the northern winter — strong evidence that distance doesn't cause the seasons.

q: Carbon dating relies on carbon-14 decaying with a half-life of roughly…
why: About 5,730 years. After death an organism stops taking in carbon-14, and it halves every 5,730 years. That makes the method useful back to about 50,000 years.

title: How a vaccine trains your immune system

steps.p: A vaccine presents a piece or blueprint of a pathogen — such as a protein from its surface — without causing the disease.
Immune cells learn to recognize that shape and produce antibodies. Some become long-lived memory cells.
When the real pathogen arrives, memory cells respond in days instead of weeks, often before you get sick.

aside: mRNA vaccines deliver instructions so your own cells briefly make the target protein, then the mRNA breaks down.

title: Why there are two high tides a day

steps.p: The Moon pulls harder on the ocean facing it than on Earth's center, and harder on Earth's center than on the far ocean.
That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges: one toward the Moon and one on the opposite side.
As Earth rotates, most coasts pass through both bulges each day, giving two high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.

aside: The Sun adds its own smaller effect. When they line up, at new and full moon, tides are strongest — spring tides.

q: Which empire covered the largest total land area in history?
why: The British Empire, at its 1920s peak about a quarter of Earth's land. The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire.

statement: Napoleon was unusually short for his time.
why: False. He was about 1.69 m (5 ft 7 in), average for a Frenchman of his era. Confusion between French and English inches, and British caricatures, spread the myth.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
detail: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, was founded in 1325, and the empire itself formed about a century later.

q: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
why: 1989, on November 9. The wall went up in 1961. Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

statement: Vikings wore horned helmets into battle.
why: False. No horned Viking battle helmet has ever been found. The image largely comes from 19th-century costume designs, including for Wagner's operas.

q: Who was the first person to travel into space?
why: Yuri Gagarin, on April 12, 1961, completing one orbit in Vostok 1. Alan Shepard became the first American in space less than a month later.

title: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid of Giza was built.
detail: A small population survived on Wrangel Island, off Siberia, until about 4,000 years ago — several centuries after the pyramid was completed around 2560 BC.

q: Which was the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
why: New Zealand. A petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered signatures from nearly a quarter of the adult female population. The UK followed in part in 1918, the US in 1920.

statement: The Hundred Years' War lasted exactly 100 years.
why: False — it lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long truces between phases. The name was given by later historians.

q: Around when did Gutenberg's printing press begin producing books in Europe?
why: Around 1450. His Bible appeared in about 1455. Within 50 years, presses had printed millions of books across Europe. Movable type had existed earlier in China and Korea.

title: The Ottoman Empire still existed when the first airplane flew.
detail: The Wright brothers flew in 1903. The Ottoman Empire, founded around 1299, was not formally dissolved until 1922.
